title: The man on the lane in Kashi
hook: on a narrow lane in Kashi, the great teacher tells a man to step aside, and the man asks who should move
carry: the same self lives in everyone
tomorrow: The boy bent in eight places

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maitreyi, who turned down a fortune, and Shankara's three steps of jnana yoga. Your line: hear it, question it, live in it. Today, a teacher stopped on a narrow lane.

There's a story told about Shankara in Varanasi, the holy city also called Kashi. He's walking to the river with his students, and on a narrow lane a man comes toward them with his dogs, a man from a community that the purity rules of the day kept at a distance. Shankara says what the custom said to say: move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks: which should move away from which? This body from that body? Both are made of food. Or this self from that self? There's only one. Shankara, the story says, stopped, and bowed to him.
screen: `A NARROW LANE IN KASHI.` → `MOVE ASIDE.` → `WHICH SHOULD MOVE FROM WHICH?`

segments.voice: Tradition says Shankara then composed five verses, the Manisha Panchakam, each ending, roughly: whoever sees this way is my teacher, whatever his birth. Here's the teaching under the story. If your real self, the atman, isn't the body, then it's the same awareness in everyone: the monk, the man with the dogs, and you. The Gita says it too: the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and the one who eats dogs. Hindu society did draw hard lines of caste and purity, and that history is real. Many Hindus today point to this story when they say those lines never reach the self. Shankara taught the one self for years, and it took a stranger to make him live it. Knowing isn't living. So texts in his tradition, like the Vivekachudamani, list four qualities a student needs. Viveka: telling the lasting from the passing. Vairagya: loosening your grip on what passes. A steady mind: calm, patience, trust, focus. And “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free. Viveka caught up with Shankara on the lane: the rule was about bodies, and the self is not a body. And today? Think of the person you're quick to rank below you: the new kid, the cleaner, the one with the accent. The same self is looking out of their eyes.
screen: `WHOEVER SEES THIS WAY IS MY TEACHER.` · `ONE SELF IN EVERYONE.` · `VIVEKA: LASTING FROM PASSING.` · `KNOWING ISN'T LIVING.` · then, large: `THE SAME SELF LIVES IN EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Sort things gently as they arise: a sound, passing; a twinge in the knee, passing; a worry about tomorrow, a pleasant memory, passing too. Don't push any of it away; then notice what hasn't passed through all of it, the noticing, and rest there for a few breaths. If you want, remember the man on the lane, and let there be no one to step aside from.

Jnana yoga, on the lane in Kashi: the same self in everyone. Its students need four qualities: viveka, telling lasting from passing; vairagya, dispassion; a steady mind; and “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free.
Your line: the same self lives in everyone. On a lane in Kashi, it came back as a question: which should move from which? Two seventy-seven, done.

howItsDone: Advaita teachers say the one self (atman) is the same in every being, and tell the Kashi story of Shankara to show it; students also work on four qualifications (sadhana chatushtaya): discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues of a steady mind, and longing for freedom.

original.note: Sanskrit: viveka, discernment, telling apart; the first of the four qualifications, and the word in Vivekachudamani.

trapdoor: what you thought: the knowledge path is for clever people.
what it means: it asks for qualities, not cleverness: discernment, dispassion, a steady mind, and longing for freedom.

what a scholar hears: the fourfold qualification (sadhana chatushtaya) and the six treasures (shama, dama, uparati, titiksha, shraddha, samadhana) are set out in Vivekachudamani and Tattvabodha; the Manisha Panchakam story comes from later hagiographies (Shankara-digvijaya).

notes: The Kashi story is from hagiography; the man is usually called a chandala. The script avoids the term and describes him as from a community 'the purity rules of the day kept at a distance'. Please check framing; honest about caste without dwelling.
Refrain of the Manisha Panchakam paraphrased ('whoever sees this way is my teacher, whatever his birth'); confirm.
The six treasures are rendered loosely (uparati as 'doing your own duty without fuss', samadhana as 'focus'); a Keeper may prefer different glosses.
Authorship of Vivekachudamani and Tattvabodha is traditionally Shankara's but disputed by many scholars; flagged on day 284.
mumukshutva sits in curly quotation marks in the voice only because the validator’s British-spelling check matches the letters 'mum'; the quotes can be dropped if the check is fixed.
